title: Mara, Part 2
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart returns to Mara, continuing a conversation from some weeks earlier, and takes up the Pali Canon stories in which Mara visits the Buddha and the bhikkhunis. Kanho cites the scholar G.P. Malalasekera's definition of Mara as death and tempter, then tells of Soma, whom Mara taunts for her "two-fingered wisdom," and Upacala, whose verse about a burning world leaves Mara no place. In each story the nun recognizes Mara, and Mara disappears sad and disappointed. To learn that recognition, Kanho offers metta meditation and mindfulness of the mind, befriending thoughts and turning away from nothing, and closes by repeating Upacala's verse.

sentences.text: Thank you, Tim, for inviting me to give a talk tonight.
As always, please consider whatever I say to be a temporary take on the state of Chris's view of the dharma.
It's very tentative and always changing, and I hope it's evolving, but I'm not so sure about it sometimes.
Some weeks ago, we talked about Mara, and I got some emails and people started some conversations about it, so I thought we might continue our conversation about my old companion, Mara.
The subject is nowhere near exhausted.
Also, I hope that there will be some time left after the talk so we can continue our discussion.
Let us start with a quick look back at who or what Mara is.

In brief, Mara stands for our obstacles or hindrances on the Buddhist path, our avoidance, the tendency to flee the difficult, to escape from reality by distracting ourselves, by seeking entertainment.
Instead of opening to emptiness, the empty nature of things, we seek security and permanence in phenomena in Mara.
In a more scholarly view, as presented by Professor G.P.

Malala Sekhera, I hope I didn't mangle his name too badly, Mara is defined as the personification of death, the evil one, the tempter, the Buddhist counterpart of the devil, or the principle of destruction.
The term Mara can be applied to the whole of worldly existence, the five aggregates, the realm of rebirth as opposed to Nirvana.
Professor Malala Sekhera writes:
*The causes enabling death to hold sway over the world.
All temptations brought about by the kleshas were likewise regarded as the work of death.

There was also evidently a legend of a devaputa of a world called Mara, who considered himself the head of the sensual realm and who recognized any attempt to curb the enjoyment of sensual pleasures as a direct challenge to himself and to his authority.
As time went on, these different conceptions of the word became confused, one with the other.*
It's quite a load.
In a way, I'm glad that I'm not a professor.
I write shorter sentences with smaller words.

But it's quite interesting how much Mara was made into another thing, how concrete he becomes in this description: death, all the beings affected by this, the head of a world system in which sense pleasure rules, someone who feels challenged by renunciation.
In the Pali Canon, the oldest of Buddhist writings, it is said that throughout the Buddha's life, Mara continues to show up to tempt, mislead and terrify the Buddha.
In all cases, the Buddha sees and understands what is happening, that this is an encounter with Mara.
He responds to Mara directly each and every time, addressing him by name: "Oh, this is Mara, the evil one."
And then the Buddha also directly names and describes and addresses the temptation, lie or delusion fabricated by Mara.

It's interesting that the next lines are the same in all the sutras: *Then Mara, the evil one, realizing the Blessed One knows me, the Fortunate One knows me, sad and disappointed, disappeared right there.* The Buddha, as we can imagine, was not the only one plagued by Mara.
Mara seemed to like visiting the nuns, the bhikkhunis, so there are many stories about Mara tempting or frightening them.
He tempts the bhikkhuni alavika with sensual pleasures.
He tried to discourage the nun Soma from practicing because as a woman, she was never going to get it for sure.
He talked to Gautami about her dead son.
Vijaya, he tries to seduce.
Uppalavanna, he tries to scare with bandits.
Upacala, he wants to influence with rebirth in the realm of gods.
Sisupacala, he wants to engage in religious debate.
Selai, he tells about independence.
Vajira, about the creator.
But all the nuns recognize Mara and firmly put him in his place.
I love the strength and poetic expression, for example, when Upacala took on Mara:
*All the world is on fire.
All the world is burning.
All the world is ablaze.
All the world is quaking.
That which does not quake or blaze.
That to which worldlings do not resort.
Where there is no place for Mara.
That is where my mind delights.*
Or Soma.
Soma was in a grove for the day's meditation when Mara appeared and addressed her:
*That state of mind, so hard to achieve, which is attained by the seers, can't be attained by a woman with her two-fingered wisdom.*
I looked this up, because "two-fingered wisdom" did not make much sense to me.
Apparently that was a phrase to describe the wisdom and knowledge of women.
One of the explanations was that the women would squeeze cooked rice between their fingers to see if it's done, and so it represents a simple-minded and limited knowledge.
Quickly, maybe using her two-fingered wisdom, Soma recognized Mara and replied:
*What does womanhood matter at all?
When the mind is concentrated well, when knowledge flows steadily, as one sees directly into Dhamma.
One to whom it might occur, I'm a woman, or I am a man, or I'm anything at all, is fit for Mara to address.*
*Then Mara, the evil one, realizing the Bhikkhuni Soma knows me, sad and disappointed, disappeared right there.*
To recognize Mara is the antidote, which brings up a new question: how can we learn to recognize Mara?
As we saw last time, Mara can be very seductive.
His storyline can be very Buddhist, and he can sound very compassionate.
In fact, Mara and the Buddha may utter exactly the same words, however with different intentions and under different circumstances.
So how do we tell them apart?
There are no Mara detectors on Amazon, or at the mall, I checked.
For myself, I've thought of two ways.
One is a non-specific application, and one is specific.
The non-specific way is metta meditation, lots of it.
May you be safe, may you be peaceful and happy, may you be healthy, may you be at ease.

Metta meditation for the self, for loved ones, for the neutral people, for people for whom we feel aversion, for groups, countries, continents, for all those who suffer from climate change, and for those who cause it.
May you be safe, may you be peaceful and happy, may you be healthy, may you be at ease.
A more specific remedy I came up with is mindfulness of the mind, the third foundation of mindfulness.
We need to discover the wakeful quality in the experience of our body, our feelings, our sense perceptions, our thoughts.
Let us befriend our thoughts, actually.
They are with us a lot, so aversion does not work.
Ignorance is not a good thing, so befriending seems to be a good idea.
Let us become very intimate with what is.
Let us become intimate with impermanence and suffering.
The practice of mindfulness of the mind involves knowing what our state of mind is, whatever it is.
Let us not turn away from anything, ever.
Let us look at it, see it, and find that this also is so.
Our bravery is the willingness to be present with our experience.
It is to sit like the Buddha under the Bodhi tree, to experience and to face whatever presents itself, and to know what it is.
And if something goes counter to this knowing what truly is, good chance it might be Mara.
Remember what the nun Upacala said: *If I do not quake with aversion or blaze with desire, there is no place for Mara.
That which does not quake or blaze, that to which worldlings do not resort, where there is no place for Mara, that is where my mind delights.* Thank you.
